The Whittaker Cookbook is filled with short and self-contained recipes that try to answer one
question at a time. Every recipe is fully executable so you can copy the code and run it easily in
your own environment.

## Getting started

Start here if you are new to Whittaker. These recipes cover the core workflow: fitting a model,
picking the right response distribution, and reading the output.

## Smooth terms

The smooth term (its basis type, basis dimension, and interaction structure) is the main modeling
decision in a GAM. These recipes cover the most useful smooth types and how to configure them.

## Response families

The response family determines the assumed distribution of your outcome and the link function that
connects it to the linear predictor. These recipes show how to handle counts, binary outcomes, and
proportions (the most common departures from a Gaussian response).

<div class="section-cards section-cards-list" style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr; gap: 1rem; margin-top: 0.5rem;">

<div style="font-size: 1.1rem; font-weight: 600; margin-bottom: 0.35rem; color: #0d6efd;">Model Count Data with Poisson</div>
<div style="font-size: 0.9rem; color: #6c757d; line-height: 1.45;">Fit a GAM when the response is a non-negative integer count, such as events per interval.</div>
</a>
</div>

## Prediction and inference

A fitted GAM is most useful when you can generate predictions at new inputs and attach uncertainty
estimates. These recipes cover point predictions, standard errors, and several flavors of confidence
interval.

criterion.

## Shape constraints

Shape-constrained smooths enforce monotone or convex behavior when domain knowledge demands it.
Use them to make a GAM obey known physical constraints while still fitting the data nonparametrically.

<div class="section-cards section-cards-list" style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr; gap: 1rem; margin-top: 0.5rem;">
<div style="border: 1px solid #dee2e6; border-radius: 0.5rem; overflow: hidden;">
<a href="fit-a-monotone-increasing-smooth.qmd" style="display: block; padding: 1.25rem 1.5rem; color: inherit; text-decoration: none;">
<div style="font-size: 1.1rem; font-weight: 600; margin-bottom: 0.35rem; color: #0d6efd;">Fit a Monotone Increasing Smooth</div>
<div style="font-size: 0.9rem; color: #6c757d; line-height: 1.45;">Constrain a smooth to be non-decreasing with bs='mpi' when the response must rise with the predictor.</div>
</a>
</div>
<div style="border: 1px solid #dee2e6; border-radius: 0.5rem; overflow: hidden;">
<a href="fit-a-monotone-decreasing-smooth.qmd" style="display: block; padding: 1.25rem 1.5rem; color: inherit; text-decoration: none;">
<div style="font-size: 1.1rem; font-weight: 600; margin-bottom: 0.35rem; color: #0d6efd;">Fit a Monotone Decreasing Smooth</div>
<div style="font-size: 0.9rem; color: #6c757d; line-height: 1.45;">Constrain a smooth to be non-increasing with bs='mpd' to model effects that can only fall.</div>
</a>
</div>
<div style="border: 1px solid #dee2e6; border-radius: 0.5rem; overflow: hidden;">
<a href="fit-a-convex-smooth.qmd" style="display: block; padding: 1.25rem 1.5rem; color: inherit; text-decoration: none;">
<div style="font-size: 1.1rem; font-weight: 600; margin-bottom: 0.35rem; color: #0d6efd;">Fit a Convex Smooth</div>
<div style="font-size: 0.9rem; color: #6c757d; line-height: 1.45;">Enforce bowl-shaped curvature with bs='cx' for responses that have a known convex structure.</div>
</a>
</div>
</div>

## Data input

Whittaker accepts Pandas DataFrames, Polars DataFrames, PyArrow Tables, plain dicts, and NumPy
arrays interchangeably. This section shows how to work with data formats you may already have on
hand, including how to account for exposure with an offset term.

## Large datasets

When data is too large to hold in memory, these approaches fit the same smooth models without
materializing the full design matrix (using discretization, DuckDB, or Polars streaming).

## Deployment

pipeline. These recipes cover serialization, scikit-learn compatibility, and R interoperability.
